description: Solo project from Kazakhstan: a web app that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one burn calendar for Central Asia, 2001 to today.
summary: Burn Calendar merges 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (2000–) and VIIRS (2012–) into a single, sensor-independent monthly fire series for Kazakhstan and Central Asia, and serves it as a free web app. VIIRS sees 3–5 times more fires than MODIS, so the two records cannot simply be joined. I calibrated MODIS against VIIRS where both exist (2012–2025), compared three statistical models with year-blocked cross-validation, and converted 2001–2011 MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent counts, cutting the bias from −73 % to −9 % and the annual error from 74 % to 13 %. Emergency services, scientists, farmers and foresters can draw any area and instantly see when it normally burns, whether this month is abnormal against a 25-year baseline, the long-term trend, and the individual hotspots, and download everything as CSV or PNG. For Kazakhstan the harmonized record reveals a 7 %-per-year decline in fire activity since the early 2000s that the raw data hide; the decline holds on observed VIIRS years alone (−7.6 %/yr, 2012–2025).
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Burn Calendar is a web application that answers three questions for any area in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan or Turkmenistan: (1) When does this place burn? A months * years burn calendar heat map from 2001 to the current month shows the fire season, its shifts and its exceptional years at a glance. (2) Is this month unusual? Every month is compared with the median, mean and interquartile range of the same calendar month across 25 years; anomalous months are flagged. (3) Is fire activity changing? Annual totals with a Theil–Sen trend and Mann–Kendall significance test, plus peak months and years.

Users select an area by drawing a rectangle, polygon or circle on the map, by typing coordinates and a radius, or by picking one of 48 administrative regions or a whole country. The map shows the individual satellite hotspots behind the numbers, coloured by sensor. All charts use colour-blind-safe scales and can be saved as PNG; detections, monthly aggregates and anomalies download as CSV. A public JSON API lets early-warning systems use the same data.

HOW IT WORKS

Data. Yearly FIRMS country archives for MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua), VIIRS 375 m S-NPP and NOAA-20 for five countries, plus the current year through the FIRMS area API (standard and near-real-time products). In total 3.9 million detections from November 2000 to November 2026.

Cleaning. MODIS detections with confidence ≥ 30 and VIIRS detections with nominal or high confidence are kept; static heat sources flagged by FIRMS (gas flares, industrial sites, volcanoes) are dropped, and near-real-time points within about 1 km of a known static source are removed. This matters in western Kazakhstan, where oil and gas flares would otherwise masquerade as winter fires.

Harmonization. Detections are counted on a 0.25° grid per month. Terra-only months before Aqua (mid-2002) are scaled by a seasonal Terra+Aqua/Terra factor. Three models that convert MODIS counts into VIIRS S-NPP-equivalent counts are fitted on the 2012–2025 overlap: a seasonal ratio, a seasonal log-linear regression, and a cell × season ratio with empirical-Bayes shrinkage. Year-blocked validation (train 2012–2018, test 2019–2025): the cell × season model wins (cell-month MAE 6.75 vs 8.41 unadjusted, regional monthly correlation 0.985, annual error 12.7 % vs 73.8 %, bias −9 % vs −73 %) and is applied to 2001–2011. From 2012 the series is VIIRS S-NPP itself, with NOAA-20 filling S-NPP outages.

App. A Python FastAPI backend answers queries from pre-aggregated Parquet files with pandas and DuckDB in under a second; polygons are intersected with the grid using fractional cell weights. The front end is a single page with Leaflet and Plotly, running in a small Docker container.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Comparable baseline: this year is measured against 25 years in the same unit. Hidden trends become visible: in Kazakhstan, harmonized detections fell from 225 000–390 000 per year in 2002–2006 to 19 000–64 000 in 2022–2025 (−7 % per year, p < 0.001); observed VIIRS years alone (2012–2025) give −7.6 % per year (p ≈ 0.05), so the decline is not a model artifact. Local answers: a fire officer can draw a district or a radius around a village. Users: emergency and early-warning services, scientists, farmers and land managers, fire services and forestry agencies.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Shapely, Matplotlib, Jupyter), FastAPI, JavaScript, Leaflet, Leaflet.draw, Plotly.js, Docker, Render, GitHub.

CREATIVITY AND LIMITATIONS

The correction varies by season and by place, with statistical shrinkage so that cells with little data stay close to the regional value; two often-ignored sensor changes (Terra-only months, S-NPP outages) are corrected. Limitations: counts are detections, not burned area; cloud cover limits all sensors. Next: add burned area (MCD64A1) as a second layer, daily NRT refresh and alerts for abnormal months.

Live app: https://burn-calendar.onrender.com
